facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest case for higher readiness is that the filings agree with themselves on the figures that drive leverage and liquidity: the debt note ties to the balance sheet at year-end 2025 and at June 2026, and the quarterly chains tie to the annual totals. That case does not reach covenant headroom, guarantor and collateral coverage or anything after June 2026, which the filings cannot settle. Readiness would rise with the credit agreement and amendments, the third-quarter 2026 report and a report on the Walker closing and funding. It would fall if the third-quarter report restated earlier periods or revised the Seemann purchase accounting again, or if the credit agreement defined the covenant differently from the filings' summary. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Leverage has risen on every measure. Total debt over reported EBITDA was 3.66x at year-end 2024, 4.17x at year-end 2025 and 4.79x on the twelve months to 30 June 2026, and net of cash it was 3.55x, 3.88x and 4.47x. On the issuer's adjusted EBITDA, net leverage was 3.27x, 3.20x and 3.94x. Pro forma for the Seemann cash paid on 3 February 2026, year-end 2025 net leverage would have been 5.63x on reported EBITDA. Total debt grew by USD 257,789 thousand in the first half of 2026, driven by a USD 265.0 million term loan increase that funded the Seemann acquisition, while the earnings base holds the acquired business only from 3 February 2026. The company states no pro forma EBITDA, so the 30 June 2026 ratio overstates run-rate leverage by an amount that is not established, and the only financial covenant, a springing test that applies when revolver loans exceed a threshold the filings do not state, was not required because the revolver was undrawn. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest contrary case is that the rise in leverage is timing: the Seemann debt was raised in February 2026 while its earnings are in the base for only part of the period, the adjusted EBITDA margin has stayed near 30%, backlog reached USD 1.3 billion at 30 June 2026 from USD 801,056 thousand at year-end 2025, and net leverage on adjusted EBITDA is 3.94x. That case wins if pro forma earnings show net leverage falling toward the year-end level and if contract assets stop growing so that operating cash flow turns positive after capital expenditure. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against a constrained view is that growth, margins and visibility are improving together: second-quarter organic growth was 24.4% by the company's account, adjusted EBITDA margin has held near 30%, the free cash outflow of the first half of 2026 was smaller than a year earlier, the 2026 outlook was raised in March, May and August 2026, and the backlog of USD 1.3 billion is about 2.21x twelve-month revenue. If the outlook is met and net debt stays at its June level, net leverage on adjusted EBITDA would fall to 3.22x, the repricing already lowers interest by about USD 3,820 thousand a year, and liquidity covers 4.06 years of the current cash outflow. The view would improve if operating cash flow turns positive after capital expenditure, if contract assets stop growing faster than revenue, if pro forma earnings show the acquired businesses covering their debt, and if the control weaknesses are reported as remediated. It would worsen if the Walker acquisition is funded with revolver or term loan before earnings, if a top-three customer delays or loses a program, if the revolver is drawn above the covenant test threshold, or if restated figures follow from the control weaknesses. facts.label: Company description
facts.text: Karman Holdings Inc. designs, tests and manufactures payload protection, aerodynamic interstage and propulsion systems for missile defense, tactical missile and space launch programs and sells mainly to prime contractors. Revenue was USD 471,500 thousand in 2025, split 31.81%, 31.78% and 36.41% across hypersonics and strategic missile defense, space and launch, and tactical missiles and integrated defense systems, and the maritime end market opened in 2026 with the Seemann acquisition. The company has grown through nine acquisitions since formation, selecting engineered products with intellectual property that can be used across programs, and it leases all of its facilities, so growth needs capital spending and lease capacity while the programs it serves are long-lived and recurring. The credit linkage is positive for cash-flow visibility and negative for liquidity preservation, because contract assets, fixed-price work and debt-funded acquisitions absorb the cash that the visibility should produce. facts.text: Karman is a listed Delaware corporation formed by the conversion of TCFIII Spaceco Holdings LLC in February 2025, and no holder, sponsor or controlling group is named in the documents supplied. facts.label: Revenue drivers and pricing power
facts.text: Revenue is driven by production volumes on missile, interceptor and launch programs, by new content on existing programs and by acquisitions, with the company reporting second-quarter 2026 organic growth of 24.4% against total growth of 58.18%. Revenue is recurring and visible because programs are long-lived and requalification is costly, but it is concentrated in three customers at 51.5% of revenue, depends on U.S. government budgets and is partly fixed-price, so cost overruns and delays sit with the company and pass-through of tariff costs is not assured. Pricing power is therefore moderate: the company can defend its sole-source positions but cannot assume price increases, which supports stable gross margins but not margin expansion beyond operating leverage. For creditors this means revenue is durable in volume terms and exposed in timing and cost terms. facts.label: Cost structure and margin resilience
facts.text: Gross margin rose to 40.30% in 2025 and 42.64% in the first half of 2026, while general and administrative expenses nearly doubled to USD 85,656 thousand in 2025, with share-based compensation of USD 8,084 thousand that the company adds back and acquisition-related costs expensed as incurred. Margins have held through rapid growth, with adjusted EBITDA margin within 1.66 percentage points over three years, but they have not been tested by falling volumes, a loss of a top customer's volume would deleverage fixed costs and the add-backs make the reported margin the safer base. The implication is that margin resilience is average, not strong. facts.label: Porter's five forces
facts.text: Rivalry is moderate: the supplier base is large and fragmented in piece parts and subsystems, with few integrated system providers, so the company competes mainly on technical content and integrated delivery, which holds prices but leaves the company exposed to the few integrated competitors. The company says the threat of new entrants is low because qualification is lengthy, programs run for decades and it holds intellectual property, which would protect revenue and support debt service if borne out. The threat of substitutes comes from customers bringing design and manufacture in-house or from government release of technical data, which would cut volumes at the primes' discretion. Buyer power is high: three customers supply 51.5% of revenue, the government can terminate contracts at its convenience and contracts are not fully funded at inception, so pricing and timing terms favor buyers. Supplier power is moderate: some components are sole-sourced and one supplier held 23.8% of payables at year-end 2025 and 12.0% at 31 March 2026, which can delay deliveries and raise cost. facts.text: Political and regulatory factors are material: the budget process has repeatedly ended in shutdowns and continuing resolutions that hold agencies to prior-year funding, and tariff rules were unsettled after the Supreme Court invalidated a significant portion of the tariffs in February 2026, which could raise costs that cannot be passed through. Economic factors are material through interest rates, because the term loan floats and carried 6.46% at 30 June 2026, and through the tight market for skilled labor. facts.label: Financial profile and credit quality
facts.text: Scale and market position are average: revenue of USD 471,500 thousand in 2025 supports a niche position in subsystems, but market share is not given and the market-leading claim is management's own. Competitive advantage is strong on documented sole-source and long-program positions, though customers hold bargaining power. Business diversification is average: three balanced end markets and no program above 12% of revenue, offset by 51.5% of revenue in three customers and one budget source. Cost and capex flexibility is average, because capital expenditure is rising to 6.56% of revenue and fixed-price work limits cost relief. Margin stability is average, strong only on the adjusted basis. Free cash flow stability is weak, at negative USD 27,671 thousand over the twelve months. Ability to refinance and access capital markets is average: the company completed an initial public offering and two secondary sales, lenders repriced twice and upsized the revolver, but there is no rating or traded debt in the documents and net leverage is 4.47x. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The most credible downside starts with a delay, de-scoping or cost overrun on a program at one of the three customers that supply 51.5% of revenue, or with a budget disruption that holds new awards, in a year when the Walker acquisition closes. Revenue and fixed-cost absorption weaken first, contract assets and receivables then build further because the two customers above 10% of revenue hold 29.7% of receivables, and free cash flow, already negative USD 24,840 thousand in the first half of 2026, worsens. If the shortfall and Walker were funded from the revolver, which is 74.35% of USD 201,741 thousand of liquidity, leverage would rise from 4.47x and the 6.50x first-lien net leverage test would come into effect once the draw passes the unstated threshold. Interest on the floating term loan costs USD 7,640 thousand a year for each 100 bp, and no bullet maturity falls due before 2030, so distress within twelve months is unlikely: liquidity equals 4.06 years of the current outflow. Management can cut capital expenditure, pause acquisitions and withhold dividends, and equity markets were open at USD 61.00 a share in May 2026; the first observable signs would be a falling backlog, rising contract assets and revolver draws. facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, Karman presents an adequate business profile supported by sole-source positions, a backlog of USD 1.3 billion and adjusted EBITDA margin near 30%, but credit quality is constrained by acquisition-funded net leverage of 4.47x, negative free cash flow and control weaknesses that are not remediated. Cash-flow durability appears weak because working capital and capital expenditure absorb the cash that EBITDA produces. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on EBITDA growth reaching the outlook, on the revolver staying available and on the interest rate, with no bullet maturity before 2030. The primary downside path is a customer or budget disruption during a debt-funded acquisition, which would raise revolver use and leverage before earnings catch up. Further analysis would require pro forma earnings, the credit agreement, ownership and the third-quarter 2026 results. Top risk: acquisition-funded leverage without free cash flow. Basis: calculation C5; calculation C7; calculation C8; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A)

# Source readiness for Karman Holdings Inc. (krmn), as of 2026-11-05
## Request

Karman Holdings Inc. (krmn), as of 2026-11-05, pathway credit_snapshot (Full credit assessment), run through Fundamental credit. Scope: whether the seven supplied filings and releases support Business & governance, Financial foundation and Fundamental credit, and what remains missing. No credit conclusion is drawn.
## Sources

No earlier module output was supplied to this module: it is the first module of the run.
## Findings
### Bottom line

The seven filed documents support Business & governance, Financial foundation and Fundamental credit on Karman Holdings Inc., with limits: evidence ends at 30 June 2026 and no executed credit agreement is supplied. Creditors should treat covenant headroom, collateral and any post-June leverage view as not established.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 29; calculation C10
Internal control over financial reporting is reported as not effective, and several printed values differ between documents, so figures are carried with their sources rather than reconciled.
### Key findings

Revenue and adjusted EBITDA can be chained without a gap from the first quarter of 2025 to the second quarter of 2026: the four 2025 quarters add exactly to the annual report figure, and the two 2026 quarters add exactly to the reported six months. The interim figures are unaudited and were prepared while the company reports unremediated material weaknesses in internal control.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 96; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 101; 10-Q_2026-03-31_krmn-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 3; 10-Q_2026-03-31_krmn-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 32; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-Q_2025-09-30_ck0002040127-20250930.htm.jsonl, page 3; 10-Q_2025-09-30_ck0002040127-20250930.htm.jsonl, page 40; EX-99.1_2026-03-25_krmn-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 9; calculation C1; calculation C2; calculation C3; calculation C4

The debt structure is known only through the company's own summaries. One Citibank credit agreement holds the term loan and a USD 150.0 million revolver, but the agreement and its five amendments are not in the set, so guarantors, collateral scope, baskets and the definition behind the only financial covenant, a springing first-lien net leverage test of 6.50x, cannot be checked. The revolver was undrawn at 30 June 2026, so the test was not required.

The latest evidence is the second-quarter 2026 report. Two events after the quarter end appear in it only as short disclosures: the 20 July 2026 agreement to buy Walker Precision Engineering for about USD 94.0 million, expected to close in the third quarter, and the 3 August 2026 amendment that cut the term loan margin by 50 bp. Whether the acquisition closed, how it was funded and what the third quarter produced are not established.

Printed values differ between documents in places that matter for debt and acquisitions. Total term loan principal after the February 2026 repricing is USD 767.8 million in the annual report and USD 772 million in the quarterly reports; the revolver maturity is printed as 1 April 2030 in one place and 30 April 2030 in another; and the Seemann Composites acquisition is dated 3 February 2026 in the filings but January 2026 in the March and May 2026 releases. Each value is carried with its source rather than chosen.

The second-quarter 2026 report corrects the purchase accounting for the Seemann Composites acquisition and restates March 2026 goodwill upward by USD 55.4 million and intangible assets downward by USD 61.0 million. The first-quarter 2026 report and the May 2026 release still show the earlier values, and the later filing controls.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 17; 10-Q_2026-03-31_krmn-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 2; EX-99.1_2026-05-12_krmn-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 7; calculation C9

The documents describe strategy, customers and risk factors in detail but do not say who owns or controls the company: sellers in the July 2025 and May 2026 secondary offerings are described only as certain existing stockholders, and directors, ownership, compensation and related-party dealings are incorporated by reference to a proxy statement that is not in the set. The chief executive also changed on 23 March 2026.
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case for higher readiness is that the filings agree with themselves on the figures that drive leverage and liquidity: the debt note ties to the balance sheet at year-end 2025 and at June 2026, and the quarterly chains tie to the annual totals. That case does not reach covenant headroom, guarantor and collateral coverage or anything after June 2026, which the filings cannot settle. Readiness would rise with the credit agreement and amendments, the third-quarter 2026 report and a report on the Walker closing and funding. It would fall if the third-quarter report restated earlier periods or revised the Seemann purchase accounting again, or if the credit agreement defined the covenant differently from the filings' summary.
Basis: calculation C1; calculation C3; calculation C5; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 17; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 19
### Limitations

No document dated after 10 August 2026 is in the set, so third-quarter 2026 results, the status of the Walker acquisition and any change to the credit agreement after 3 August 2026 are not established as of 5 November 2026.

Letters of credit, interest rate hedges, pension deficits and purchase commitments were searched for in every document and none was found, and the only mention of receivable sales is a general statement that they may be used if necessary; these are findings about the documents, not proof that no such claims exist.
The run settings leave credit ratings, market quotes, peer data, portfolio limits and legal documents blank, and blank is treated as not supplied rather than zero.

# Financial foundation for Karman Holdings Inc. (krmn), as of 2026-11-05
## Request

Karman Holdings Inc. (krmn), as of 2026-11-05, pathway credit_snapshot (Full credit assessment). Scope: financial foundation from the supplied annual report, three quarterly reports and three earnings releases, covering statements, debt, leverage, cover and liquidity. No credit recommendation is made.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Karman's leverage rose to 4.79x reported EBITDA at 30 June 2026 from 4.17x at year-end 2025 because acquisition debt arrived before the acquired earnings and operating cash flow was negative in 2025 and in the first half of 2026. Deleveraging therefore rests on earnings growth and backlog conversion, not on cash generation.
Basis: calculation C3; calculation C6; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 4; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 112–115

Net debt was USD 705,196 thousand at 30 June 2026 against USD 465,189 thousand at year-end 2025. With the Seemann acquisition paid for after year-end, pro forma year-end net debt was USD 675,189 thousand, or 5.63x year-end reported EBITDA that holds none of the acquired earnings. Finance leases of USD 102,139 thousand are outside these figures.
Basis: calculation C1; calculation C9; calculation C10; calculation C14; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 18
### Key findings

Leverage has risen on every measure. Total debt over reported EBITDA was 3.66x at year-end 2024, 4.17x at year-end 2025 and 4.79x on the twelve months to 30 June 2026, and net of cash it was 3.55x, 3.88x and 4.47x. On the issuer's adjusted EBITDA, net leverage was 3.27x, 3.20x and 3.94x. Pro forma for the Seemann cash paid on 3 February 2026, year-end 2025 net leverage would have been 5.63x on reported EBITDA. Total debt grew by USD 257,789 thousand in the first half of 2026, driven by a USD 265.0 million term loan increase that funded the Seemann acquisition, while the earnings base holds the acquired business only from 3 February 2026. The company states no pro forma EBITDA, so the 30 June 2026 ratio overstates run-rate leverage by an amount that is not established, and the only financial covenant, a springing test that applies when revolver loans exceed a threshold the filings do not state, was not required because the revolver was undrawn.

Basis: calculation C2; calculation C3; calculation C4; calculation C6; calculation C10; calculation C14; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 15–16; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 18–19; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 101; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 107–108

Interest cover is modest but improving. Reported EBITDA covered cash interest 2.05x in 2024, 2.67x in 2025 and 2.97x on the twelve months to 30 June 2026, with cash interest paid of USD 53,144 thousand over that period. The August 2026 amendment cut the term loan margin by 50 bp, which lowers the interest burden but is in no period figure yet.

Basis: calculation C2; calculation C5; calculation C14; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 115

Cash generation does not support deleveraging yet. Operating cash flow was negative at USD 22,119 thousand in 2025 and negative at USD 2,975 thousand in the first half of 2026, although adjusted EBITDA was USD 145,302 thousand in 2025, mainly because contract assets absorbed cash: they rose USD 49,076 thousand in 2025 and stood at USD 187,120 thousand at 30 June 2026. After capital expenditure, free cash flow was negative at USD 42,455 thousand in 2025 and negative at USD 24,840 thousand in the first half of 2026, so the cash shortfall and the acquisitions were funded by borrowing and, in 2025, by equity. Contract liabilities, the customer advances that fund part of working capital, were USD 22,814 thousand at year-end 2025 against USD 29,868 thousand a year earlier, a smaller float from customers.
Basis: calculation C8; calculation C13; calculation C14; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 113–115; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 2–4

Liquidity is adequate near term and only scheduled amortization falls due before 2030. Cash was USD 51,741 thousand and the undrawn revolver USD 150.0 million, giving liquidity of USD 201,741 thousand at 30 June 2026 against USD 83,959 thousand at year-end 2025. Scheduled principal repayments were USD 5,050 thousand a year to 2030 at year-end 2025, a schedule that predates the February 2026 term loan increase and has not been restated, and the revolver matures in 2030 and the term loan on 1 April 2032. No letters of credit were found, and the conditions for drawing the revolver are not supplied.

### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest contrary case is that the rise in leverage is timing: the Seemann debt was raised in February 2026 while its earnings are in the base for only part of the period, the adjusted EBITDA margin has stayed near 30%, backlog reached USD 1.3 billion at 30 June 2026 from USD 801,056 thousand at year-end 2025, and net leverage on adjusted EBITDA is 3.94x. That case wins if pro forma earnings show net leverage falling toward the year-end level and if contract assets stop growing so that operating cash flow turns positive after capital expenditure. It loses if working capital keeps absorbing cash, if the Walker acquisition adds debt before earnings, or if the credit agreement's covenant definition proves tighter than the filings' summary.

## Gaps

- The balance sheet at 31 December 2023 is not supplied, so the 2023 balance sheet column is absent and only the closing cash of USD 5.455 million is known from the cash flow statement; the action that would close it is the 2024 annual report. Severity: Low.

- No source states the legal ranking, guarantor scope or lien scope of the term loan, the revolver or the other notes, so the debt stack is not drawn and no secured or senior subtotal is stated; the action is the executed credit agreement and its amendments. Severity: High.

- The company states no pro forma EBITDA for the Seemann acquisition, so leverage at 30 June 2026 cannot be put on a full-year perimeter and the pro forma net leverage row uses year-end EBITDA without acquired earnings; the action is a pro forma earnings statement. Severity: High.

- The Walker acquisition is agreed but not closed in the sources read, and its funding is not described, so its effect on net debt is not stated; the action is the report on its closing and funding. Severity: High.
- No documents after the second-quarter 2026 report are supplied, so third-quarter 2026 figures are not established; the action is the third-quarter report. Severity: Medium.

- The cash flow statements print a dash for lines with no activity in a period, and the dashes are treated as missing values; the lines are listed in the cash flow table and the annual statements carry no separate line for gains or losses on asset sales. Severity: Low.

- Revenue by end market is not printed for 2023, and the Maritime Defense Systems end market has no comparable figure before 2026, so end-market growth for it is not stated; the action is a recast of the 2025 end-market series. Severity: Medium.

- The interim balance sheet prints no subtotal of long-term liabilities and no common stock existed before the offering conversion, so those two cells are not supplied; the effect is limited to presentation. Severity: Low.

- Capital expenditure is not split between maintenance and growth, and no letters of credit, hedges or purchase commitments were found, so free cash flow is stated before that split; the action is management disclosure of maintenance capital spending. Severity: Low.

- The term loan principal after the February 2026 amendment is printed as USD 767.8 million in the annual report and USD 772 million in the quarterly reports, and the scheduled amortization after that amendment is not stated; the action is the amended credit agreement. Severity: Medium.

- The initial public offering net proceeds are printed with four different figures, and the offering amount raised stated in the March release is not reconciled to them; this affects equity, not debt. Severity: Low.

# Business and governance for Karman Holdings Inc. (krmn), as of 2026-11-05
## Request

Karman Holdings Inc. (krmn), as of 2026-11-05, pathway credit_snapshot (Full credit assessment). Scope: business, ownership, operating model, issuer history and governance behavior from the supplied annual report, three quarterly reports and three earnings releases. No credit recommendation is made.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Karman is a sole- and single-source supplier to missile and space programs with a growing backlog, but three customers supply about half of revenue, acquisitions are debt-funded and internal control weaknesses remain, so governance risk is medium and provisional.

No document names who controls the company, so the view rests on issuer behavior: no dividend is planned, lenders cut the term loan margin twice, and a rising term loan funded four acquisitions since April 2025.
Basis: calculation C1; calculation C7; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 81; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 87; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 18–21
### Key findings

Demand visibility is strong but concentrated in a few prime contractors. The company holds sole- or single-source positions on many programs and estimates that no single program exceeded 12% of revenue in 2025, yet three customers supplied 51.5% of revenue in 2025 and two held 40.7% of receivables at year-end 2025. In the first half of 2026 two customers were above 10% of revenue and held 29.7% of receivables at 30 June 2026. A delay or loss at one prime would hit earnings and cash collection together. Backlog, the value of existing contracts less amounts already invoiced, rose to USD 1.3 billion at 30 June 2026 from USD 801,056 thousand at year-end 2025, which supports 2026 revenue, although the U.S. government may terminate contracts at its convenience.

The acquisition program is the main driver of governance risk. Four acquisitions since April 2025 carried a combined fair value of consideration of USD 470,428 thousand and were funded by term loan increases, with some shares; a fifth, Walker, was agreed in July 2026 for about USD 94.0 million. The term loan started at USD 300.0 million and was raised by USD 75.0 million, USD 130.0 million and USD 265.0 million, and USD 764.0 million was outstanding at 30 June 2026. Debt arrives before acquired earnings, and integration costs are added back to adjusted EBITDA, so leverage tolerance is high. Seemann contributed USD 63.0 million of revenue in the first half of 2026, 18.90% of the total, but no pro forma earnings are given for any acquisition, so payback cannot be tested.

Basis: calculation C1; calculation C4; calculation C8; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 140; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 11–18; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 29; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 35

The record on distributions and lender treatment is creditor-friendly so far. No dividend or fee to owners is documented, the company expects to retain earnings, and lenders accepted margin cuts of 75 bp in February 2026 and 50 bp in August 2026 and a revolver of USD 150.0 million. The secondary offerings in July 2025 and May 2026, priced at USD 49.00 and USD 61.00 a share, were sales by existing stockholders with no proceeds to the company, so they changed holder liquidity but not the capital structure.

Basis: calculation C5; calculation C7; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 87; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 4; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 18–21; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 25

Reporting controls are a clear governance weakness. Management reports that internal control over financial reporting was not effective at year-end 2025 and that disclosure controls were not effective at 30 June 2026 because of the same material weaknesses, which led to material adjustments to share-based compensation in 2023 and immaterial ones in 2025 and in the first half of 2026. The company says its information technology controls work is complete and the other remediation is still being implemented and tested, and the Seemann purchase price allocation was revised in the second quarter. The audit opinion on the statements is unqualified and gives no view on internal control, so lenders should treat interim figures as provisional until remediation is tested.

Who controls Karman is not established. The documents describe a classified board whose directors can be removed only for cause by a supermajority, a stockholder rights agreement and a registration rights agreement with certain investors, and unnamed selling stockholders, but they give no holdings, board seats or consent rights. The chief executive changed on 23 March 2026. Without the stockholder agreement and the proxy statement, sponsor willingness and capacity to extract value cannot be assessed, so the risk level rests on issuer behavior alone and is provisional.

Operating pressure points are fixed-price exposure and working capital. Multi-year fixed-price contracts leave cost overruns with the company, contract assets rose USD 49,076 thousand in 2025 and absorbed operating cash, and capital expenditure of USD 21,865 thousand in the first half of 2026 was 6.56% of revenue against 4.31% in 2025. Growth is therefore consuming cash ahead of billing while debt has funded the acquisitions.

Basis: calculation C6; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 31; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 114–115; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 4
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case for lower risk is the behavior record: no distributions or fees to owners are documented, lenders accepted two margin cuts and a larger revolver, equity was raised at the initial public offering, none of the documents describes an amendment or exchange that disadvantages lenders, and backlog reached USD 1.3 billion. That case wins if the proxy statement and stockholder agreements show no controlling holder with extraction incentives and if pro forma earnings show the acquired businesses covering the new debt. The case for higher risk wins if the stockholder agreements give a holder control over financing, if the Walker acquisition is funded with further term loan before earnings, or if the control weaknesses lead to restated figures.
### Limitations
- The proxy statement and the stockholder agreements are not supplied, so the ownership, board and fee findings are provisional and could move the governance risk level up or down.

- The credit agreement is not supplied, so which distributions, investments and new debt the company may make is not established, and the conclusion that no creditor-adverse behavior is documented covers only the behavior actually described.

- Customer and program names and contract terms are not disclosed, so the concentration conclusion rests on the company's own percentages and program estimate and cannot say which primes carry the revenue.

- Management descriptions such as market-leading position and difficult requalification are the company's own language and are not independently verified, so the revenue visibility conclusion is bounded by them.
- Developments after the second-quarter 2026 report, including whether Walker closed and how it was funded, are not covered, so the acquisition-appetite conclusion may be out of date.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

The company completed its initial public offering in February 2025, selling 8.4 million of the 26.5 million shares at USD 22.00, and on 1 April 2025 replaced its earlier lender with a Citibank credit agreement made up of a USD 300.0 million term loan maturing in April 2032 and a USD 50.0 million revolver. New debt since then is the term loan increases, each tied to an acquisition: USD 75.0 million in May 2025 for ISP, USD 130.0 million in October 2025 for Five Axis and the revolver repayment, and USD 265.0 million in February 2026 for Seemann Composites and MSC. The revolver commitment was raised to USD 150.0 million in March 2026 and nothing was drawn in the first half of 2026.

Fair values of consideration were USD 82.3 million for MTI, USD 58.6 million for ISP, USD 96.6 million for Five Axis and USD 232.9 million for Seemann, together USD 470.4 million, and the Walker agreement of July 2026 for about USD 94.0 million is expected to close in the third quarter of 2026 with funding not described. No bond or note issue appears in the documents; the new borrowing is under the one credit agreement, which is not itself supplied, and other notes payable were USD 4,516 thousand at 30 June 2026.

# Fundamental credit for Karman Holdings Inc. (krmn), as of 2026-11-05
## Request

Karman Holdings Inc. (krmn), as of 2026-11-05, pathway credit_snapshot (Full credit assessment). Scope: the fundamental credit synthesis of business quality, margins, cash conversion, liquidity, refinancing capacity and financial policy from the supplied annual report, three quarterly reports and three earnings releases, together with the supplied analyses of source availability, the financial statements and business and governance. No rating, security recommendation, legal-capacity conclusion or portfolio sizing is made.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Karman is a high-growth, sole-source defense and space supplier whose credit quality is constrained by acquisition-funded leverage and negative free cash flow, so creditors depend on earnings growth, not cash generation, to bring leverage down.
Basis: calculation C5; calculation C7; Financial foundation (CP-1)

Net debt was USD 705,196 thousand at 30 June 2026, 4.47x reported EBITDA for the twelve months, while free cash flow was negative USD 27,671 thousand over the same period. Liquidity of USD 201,741 thousand, a backlog of USD 1.3 billion and no bullet maturity before 2030 give creditors time, but the cushion shrinks if the pending Walker acquisition is debt-funded before its earnings arrive.

Basis: calculation C5; calculation C7; calculation C8; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 29; EX-99.1_2026-08-06_krmn-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, pages 1–2
### Key findings

The business profile is average to strong, because sole- and single-source positions on long-lived programs and a rising order book give revenue visibility. Revenue grew 36.57% in 2025 and 54.85% in the first half of 2026, the company puts second-quarter organic growth at 24.4% without defining it, and backlog rose from USD 801,056 thousand at year-end 2025 to USD 1.3 billion at 30 June 2026. Programs can run for more than 20 years and the company says customers rarely requalify a supplier, so contracted work should convert into earnings that service debt, but the government may terminate contracts and its contracts are generally not fully funded at inception, so backlog measures visibility and not cash, and the company dropped the word funded from its backlog label in 2025 without restating amounts.

Margins are stable on the company's adjusted measure and thinner on reported earnings, so leverage should be sized on the reported figure. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 29.16% in 2023, 30.74% in 2024, 30.82% in 2025 and 29.82% in the first half of 2026 against 30.48% a year earlier, while reported EBITDA margin was 27.16%, 28.39%, 25.41% and 26.30%. Add-backs of USD 25,476 thousand in 2025 were 17.53% of adjusted EBITDA and mostly acquisition costs and share-based compensation, and integration costs are still added back, so the adjusted margin is a less conservative measure of recurring cash earnings while the acquisition program continues. Gross margin rose from 37.60% in 2023 to 40.30% in 2025 and 42.64% in the first half of 2026, the clearest sign of operating leverage.

Basis: calculation C2; calculation C3; calculation C4; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 99; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 101; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 113; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 35; EX-99.1_2026-08-06_krmn-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 8

Cash conversion is the weakest dimension, because EBITDA is not yet turning into free cash flow. Operating cash flow was negative USD 22,119 thousand in 2025 and negative USD 2,975 thousand in the first half of 2026, and free cash flow after capital expenditure, positive USD 11,393 thousand in 2024, was negative USD 42,455 thousand in 2025 and negative USD 24,840 thousand in the first half of 2026, a smaller outflow than the negative USD 39,624 thousand of the first half of 2025 and negative USD 27,671 thousand over the twelve months to 30 June 2026. Growth absorbs cash before it is billed: in the first half of 2026 receivables took USD 25,455 thousand and contract assets USD 24,851 thousand, and capital expenditure rose from 4.31% of revenue in 2025 to 6.56%. Debt, not cash flow, has therefore funded the acquisitions and the shortfall, and deleveraging depends on EBITDA growth and on working capital turning.
Basis: calculation C5; calculation C6; calculation C13; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 114–115; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 4

Leverage is high for a company with negative free cash flow and was built faster than earnings. Net debt was USD 705,196 thousand at 30 June 2026, 4.47x reported EBITDA and 3.94x adjusted EBITDA for the twelve months, and finance leases of USD 102,139 thousand outside those figures take net leverage to 5.11x. Year-end 2025 net leverage was 3.88x on net debt of USD 465,189 thousand and, pro forma for the Seemann acquisition paid for on 3 February 2026, USD 675,189 thousand and 5.63x on earnings that hold none of the acquired business. If the 2026 outlook of USD 215.0 million to USD 222.5 million of adjusted EBITDA is met and net debt does not rise, net leverage would be 3.22x on that measure, but the outlook excludes any future acquisition.

Basis: calculation C7; calculation C9; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 18; EX-99.1_2026-08-06_krmn-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2

Liquidity is adequate and refinancing risk is low before 2030, but both rest on the revolver and on a floating-rate term loan. Cash of USD 51,741 thousand and the undrawn revolver of USD 150.0 million give liquidity of USD 201,741 thousand, which equals 4.06 years of the first-half free cash outflow at an annual pace, and 74.35% of it is the revolver. Only scheduled amortization falls due before the revolver matures in 2030 and the term loan on 1 April 2032, the term loan bore 6.46% at 30 June 2026, and the August 2026 amendment lowers the margin by 50 bp, worth about USD 3,820 thousand a year and lifting cash interest cover from 2.97x to 3.20x. The only financial covenant, 6.50x first-lien net leverage, applies when the revolver is drawn above a threshold the filings do not state, so headroom is not calculable.

Basis: calculation C8; calculation C11; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 107; 10-K_2025-12-31_krmn-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 140–141; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 18–19; 10-Q_2026-06-30_krmn-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 25

Concentration in a few prime contractors limits diversification and ties earnings and receivables to the same counterparties. Three customers supplied 51.5% of revenue in 2025, two customers held 40.7% of receivables at year-end 2025 and 29.7% at 30 June 2026, and the company estimates that no single program exceeded 12% of revenue. Revenue is balanced across three end markets (31.81%, 31.78% and 36.41% in 2025) and a maritime end market added USD 59,970 thousand in the first half of 2026, but all of it rests on U.S. defense and space budgets, so a delay at one prime would hit earnings and cash collection together.

Financial policy and governance are the open question: policy is acquisitive and unremediated control weaknesses leave reported figures provisional, while the record on distributions is creditor-friendly. ### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a constrained view is that growth, margins and visibility are improving together: second-quarter organic growth was 24.4% by the company's account, adjusted EBITDA margin has held near 30%, the free cash outflow of the first half of 2026 was smaller than a year earlier, the 2026 outlook was raised in March, May and August 2026, and the backlog of USD 1.3 billion is about 2.21x twelve-month revenue. If the outlook is met and net debt stays at its June level, net leverage on adjusted EBITDA would fall to 3.22x, the repricing already lowers interest by about USD 3,820 thousand a year, and liquidity covers 4.06 years of the current cash outflow. The view would improve if operating cash flow turns positive after capital expenditure, if contract assets stop growing faster than revenue, if pro forma earnings show the acquired businesses covering their debt, and if the control weaknesses are reported as remediated. It would worsen if the Walker acquisition is funded with revolver or term loan before earnings, if a top-three customer delays or loses a program, if the revolver is drawn above the covenant test threshold, or if restated figures follow from the control weaknesses.

### Limitations

- No peer, rating or market-pricing information is supplied, so the finding that leverage is high rests on the company's own history and the disclosed covenant level, and it could prove softer or harder against comparable issuers.

- The 2026 outlook and the organic growth rate are the company's own statements and the filings define neither the acquired-revenue split nor the outlook beyond excluding future acquisitions, so the outlook-implied leverage and the durability of growth rest on management's figures.

- Pro forma earnings are not stated for any acquisition, so the pro forma net leverage uses year-end earnings with none of the acquired business and overstates run-rate leverage by an amount that is not established.

- The credit agreement is not supplied, so covenant headroom, the springing-test threshold, guarantor scope and debt ranking cannot be tested, and the liquidity finding counts the whole revolver as available.

- The as-of date falls after the third quarter of 2026 but the documents end at 30 June 2026, so third-quarter results, the Walker closing and any later financing are not captured and could change the leverage and cash conversion findings.

- The company dropped the word funded from its backlog label in the annual report and now defines backlog as the total or current estimated value of contracts less amounts invoiced, with no restatement and no split of funded from unfunded work, so how much of the USD 1.3 billion is funded is not established and the revenue visibility finding cannot be turned into expected cash.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strength one is the sole- and single-source position on long-lived programs: the company holds such positions on many programs, programs can run for more than 20 years and requalification is costly, so revenue persists once a program is in production, which supports debt service across a downturn in any one end market.

Strength two is the order book: backlog of USD 801,056 thousand at year-end 2025 rose to USD 1.3 billion at 30 June 2026, about 2.21x twelve-month revenue, which gives visibility into the 2026 outlook and supports leverage coming down if conversion to revenue holds.

### Company description

Karman Holdings Inc. designs, tests and manufactures payload protection, aerodynamic interstage and propulsion systems for missile defense, tactical missile and space launch programs and sells mainly to prime contractors. Revenue was USD 471,500 thousand in 2025, split 31.81%, 31.78% and 36.41% across hypersonics and strategic missile defense, space and launch, and tactical missiles and integrated defense systems, and the maritime end market opened in 2026 with the Seemann acquisition. The company has grown through nine acquisitions since formation, selecting engineered products with intellectual property that can be used across programs, and it leases all of its facilities, so growth needs capital spending and lease capacity while the programs it serves are long-lived and recurring. The credit linkage is positive for cash-flow visibility and negative for liquidity preservation, because contract assets, fixed-price work and debt-funded acquisitions absorb the cash that the visibility should produce.

### Ownership and group structure

Karman is a listed Delaware corporation formed by the conversion of TCFIII Spaceco Holdings LLC in February 2025, and no holder, sponsor or controlling group is named in the documents supplied. Existing stockholders sold shares in secondary offerings in July 2025 and May 2026 without any proceeds to the company, a stockholder rights agreement and a registration rights agreement exist with certain investors, and directors, ownership and related-party dealings are incorporated by reference to a proxy statement that is not supplied. The board is classified, with removal only for cause on a supermajority vote, which lowers takeover pressure and lets the board issue preferred stock without a stockholder vote, so a change of control is unlikely near term and creditor protection rests on the credit agreement, which is not supplied. No restricted group, guarantor or structurally senior debt is described in the documents supplied, so structural priority is not established.

### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue is driven by production volumes on missile, interceptor and launch programs, by new content on existing programs and by acquisitions, with the company reporting second-quarter 2026 organic growth of 24.4% against total growth of 58.18%. Revenue is recurring and visible because programs are long-lived and requalification is costly, but it is concentrated in three customers at 51.5% of revenue, depends on U.S. government budgets and is partly fixed-price, so cost overruns and delays sit with the company and pass-through of tariff costs is not assured. Pricing power is therefore moderate: the company can defend its sole-source positions but cannot assume price increases, which supports stable gross margins but not margin expansion beyond operating leverage. For creditors this means revenue is durable in volume terms and exposed in timing and cost terms.

### Cost structure and margin resilience

Gross margin rose to 40.30% in 2025 and 42.64% in the first half of 2026, while general and administrative expenses nearly doubled to USD 85,656 thousand in 2025, with share-based compensation of USD 8,084 thousand that the company adds back and acquisition-related costs expensed as incurred. Engineering labor and raw materials such as composites, metals and energetic materials are the main inputs, raw materials are generally available from several suppliers but some components come from sole-source suppliers, and fixed-price work leaves overruns with the company. Margins have held through rapid growth, with adjusted EBITDA margin within 1.66 percentage points over three years, but they have not been tested by falling volumes, a loss of a top customer's volume would deleverage fixed costs and the add-backs make the reported margin the safer base. The implication is that margin resilience is average, not strong.

### Capital intensity and FCF conversion

Capital expenditure was 4.31% of revenue in 2025 and 6.56% in the first half of 2026, although the annual report says the company keeps capital expenditure low, and the filings do not split maintenance from growth spending. Working capital is the larger drain: contract assets rose USD 49,076 thousand in 2025, receivables and contract assets took USD 50,306 thousand in the first half of 2026, and cash interest was USD 53,144 thousand over the twelve months. Operating cash flow over reported EBITDA was -18.46% in 2025 and 3.71% over the twelve months to 30 June 2026, and free cash flow was negative USD 27,671 thousand, so EBITDA does not yet translate into free cash flow for debt reduction or liquidity. Capital expenditure is a lever management has, but it has been rising, so FCF durability is weak.

### Porter's five forces

Rivalry is moderate: the supplier base is large and fragmented in piece parts and subsystems, with few integrated system providers, so the company competes mainly on technical content and integrated delivery, which holds prices but leaves the company exposed to the few integrated competitors. The company says the threat of new entrants is low because qualification is lengthy, programs run for decades and it holds intellectual property, which would protect revenue and support debt service if borne out. The threat of substitutes comes from customers bringing design and manufacture in-house or from government release of technical data, which would cut volumes at the primes' discretion. Buyer power is high: three customers supply 51.5% of revenue, the government can terminate contracts at its convenience and contracts are not fully funded at inception, so pricing and timing terms favor buyers. Supplier power is moderate: some components are sole-sourced and one supplier held 23.8% of payables at year-end 2025 and 12.0% at 31 March 2026, which can delay deliveries and raise cost.
### PEST analysis

Political and regulatory factors are material: the budget process has repeatedly ended in shutdowns and continuing resolutions that hold agencies to prior-year funding, and tariff rules were unsettled after the Supreme Court invalidated a significant portion of the tariffs in February 2026, which could raise costs that cannot be passed through. Economic factors are material through interest rates, because the term loan floats and carried 6.46% at 30 June 2026, and through the tight market for skilled labor. Social and technological factors are secondary to the credit case: hypersonics and missile defense programs are a source of demand, not of disruption. Political and economic factors therefore affect cash timing and interest cost more than they affect the demand case.

### SWOT analysis

Strengths are sole-source positions on long-lived programs, a backlog of USD 1.3 billion, adjusted EBITDA margin near 30% and liquidity of USD 201,741 thousand. Weaknesses are net leverage of 4.47x, negative free cash flow, customer concentration of 51.5% in three customers and controls that are not effective. Opportunities that could improve credit quality are the raised 2026 outlook converting into the 3.22x outlook-implied leverage, the August 2026 repricing, and prime awards for interceptors and submarines that management cites. Threats that could weaken it are a debt-funded Walker acquisition, a budget disruption that delays awards and cash, rising rates on floating debt and restated figures from the control weaknesses.

### Financial profile and credit quality

Scale and market position are average: revenue of USD 471,500 thousand in 2025 supports a niche position in subsystems, but market share is not given and the market-leading claim is management's own. Competitive advantage is strong on documented sole-source and long-program positions, though customers hold bargaining power. Business diversification is average: three balanced end markets and no program above 12% of revenue, offset by 51.5% of revenue in three customers and one budget source. Cost and capex flexibility is average, because capital expenditure is rising to 6.56% of revenue and fixed-price work limits cost relief. Margin stability is average, strong only on the adjusted basis. Free cash flow stability is weak, at negative USD 27,671 thousand over the twelve months. Ability to refinance and access capital markets is average: the company completed an initial public offering and two secondary sales, lenders repriced twice and upsized the revolver, but there is no rating or traded debt in the documents and net leverage is 4.47x. Liquidity is average, because 74.35% of it is the revolver and the Walker acquisition is pending. Financial policy and governance are weak for now, given acquisition-funded leverage, no stated leverage target, ineffective controls and an unidentified controlling holder. The trend is improving in earnings and in the free cash outflow, which narrowed in the first half of 2026, and worsening in leverage, and the missing data are pro forma earnings, the credit agreement, ownership and third-quarter 2026 results.

### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

For the next twelve to 24 months the company guides 2026 revenue to USD 730 million to USD 745 million and adjusted EBITDA to USD 215.0 million to USD 222.5 million, excluding future acquisitions, which implies adjusted margin of 29.45% to 29.87% and second-half revenue of USD 396,727 thousand to USD 411,727 thousand, so second-half revenue must run 19.04% to 23.54% above the first half. The outlook was raised in March, May and August 2026, the backlog and the repricing support it, and Walker adds European defense exposure with funding not described. Over three to five years the demand case rests on interceptor and submarine awards and the Golden Dome program, which support volumes and margin if the primes pass work down, while headwinds are budget disruption, tariffs, labor and integration of four completed acquisitions and the pending Walker deal. Company-specific tailwinds support revenue and refinancing confidence, and headwinds pressure free cash flow and leverage.

### Downside scenario

The most credible downside starts with a delay, de-scoping or cost overrun on a program at one of the three customers that supply 51.5% of revenue, or with a budget disruption that holds new awards, in a year when the Walker acquisition closes. Revenue and fixed-cost absorption weaken first, contract assets and receivables then build further because the two customers above 10% of revenue hold 29.7% of receivables, and free cash flow, already negative USD 24,840 thousand in the first half of 2026, worsens. If the shortfall and Walker were funded from the revolver, which is 74.35% of USD 201,741 thousand of liquidity, leverage would rise from 4.47x and the 6.50x first-lien net leverage test would come into effect once the draw passes the unstated threshold. Interest on the floating term loan costs USD 7,640 thousand a year for each 100 bp, and no bullet maturity falls due before 2030, so distress within twelve months is unlikely: liquidity equals 4.06 years of the current outflow. Management can cut capital expenditure, pause acquisitions and withhold dividends, and equity markets were open at USD 61.00 a share in May 2026; the first observable signs would be a falling backlog, rising contract assets and revolver draws.

### Overall credit view

Overall, Karman presents an adequate business profile supported by sole-source positions, a backlog of USD 1.3 billion and adjusted EBITDA margin near 30%, but credit quality is constrained by acquisition-funded net leverage of 4.47x, negative free cash flow and control weaknesses that are not remediated. Cash-flow durability appears weak because working capital and capital expenditure absorb the cash that EBITDA produces. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on EBITDA growth reaching the outlook, on the revolver staying available and on the interest rate, with no bullet maturity before 2030. The primary downside path is a customer or budget disruption during a debt-funded acquisition, which would raise revolver use and leverage before earnings catch up. Further analysis would require pro forma earnings, the credit agreement, ownership and the third-quarter 2026 results. Top risk: acquisition-funded leverage without free cash flow.

## Gaps

- The credit agreement and its amendments are not supplied, so the springing-test threshold, covenant definitions and headroom, guarantor scope, debt ranking and amortization after February 2026 are not established; the action is the executed agreement. Severity: High.

- No pro forma earnings are stated for the acquired businesses, so leverage after the Seemann acquisition cannot be put on a full-year basis; the action is a pro forma statement or management bridge. Severity: High.

- Who owns and controls the company is not established because the proxy statement and the stockholder agreements are not supplied; the action is the 2026 proxy statement and the agreements. Severity: High.
- The Walker acquisition is agreed but its closing and funding are not described, so its effect on leverage and liquidity is not established; the action is the report on its closing. Severity: High.

- No rating, peer or traded-debt information is supplied, so leverage and margins cannot be compared with similar issuers and market access is judged from the company's own transactions; the action is rating and peer data. Severity: Medium.

- Organic growth is stated by the company without a definition and the split of acquired revenue is stated only for Seemann, so growth in existing programs is not established beyond the second quarter; the action is a disclosure of acquired revenue by acquisition. Severity: Medium.

- The funded and unfunded parts of backlog are not stated, and the label changed from funded backlog in the 2025 quarterly reports to backlog in the annual report with a wider definition and unchanged amounts, so the cash that backlog represents is not established; the action is management disclosure of funded backlog. Severity: Medium.
- Capital expenditure is not split between maintenance and growth, so the flexibility of capital expenditure in a downturn is not established; the action is management disclosure. Severity: Low.
- No documents after the second-quarter 2026 report are supplied, so third-quarter 2026 results are not established; the action is the third-quarter 2026 reports. Severity: Medium.

- The revolver maturity is printed as 1 April 2030 in one place and 30 April 2030 in another, and the term loan principal after February 2026 is printed as USD 767.8 million and USD 772 million; the later quarterly figures are used and the difference is not explained. Severity: Low.
